title: Permutation Edit Distance
statementMd:
You are given two permutations∗∗ and must compute the edit distance between them using only the following edits:

- Given a length n𝑛 permutation, insert n+1𝑛+1 anywhere into the array, resulting in a permutation of length n+1.
- Given a length n permutation, delete n from the array, resulting in a permutation of length n−1.

The edit distance between two permutations p and q is the minimum possible number of edits it takes to turn p into q or vice versa. It can be shown that, given the edits above, it does not matter which permutation you start with.

∗A permutation of length n is an array consisting of n distinct integers from 1 to n in arbitrary order. For example, [2,3,1,5,4] is a permutation, but [1,2,2] is not a permutation (2 appears twice in the array), and [1,3,4] is also not a permutation (n=3 but there is 4 in the array).

## Input

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases t (1≤t≤2⋅105). The description of the test cases follows.

The first line of each test case contains two integers n and m (1≤n,m≤2⋅105) — the lengths of the permutations.

The second line of each test case contains n integers p1,p2,…,pn (1≤pi≤n) — the permutation p.

The last line of each test case contains m integers q1,q2,…,qm (1≤qi≤m) — the permutation q.

It is guaranteed that the sum of max(n,m) over all test cases does not exceed 2⋅105.

## Output

For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum number of valid edits to transform p into q.

## Note

In the first test case, inserting 5 into p in the second position will result in q.

In the second test case, first delete 3 and 2 from the end of p. Then insert 2 into the beginning, and after that insert 3 into the beginning as well. This will result in q, and it can be shown that this is a minimal solution.

In the third test case, the permutations are already equal.
